title: Indian Banks Are Offering NRIs Up to 7% on Dollar Deposits. Here Is How to Get the Best Rate Before September.
excerpt: The RBI's unprecedented forex swap has sparked a rate war among banks. Emkay calculates leveraged returns could reach 22%. The window closes September 30.
body:
If you are an NRI with dollars sitting in a US savings account earning 4%, you now have a window — closing September 30 — to earn significantly more by parking them in an Indian bank's FCNR(B) deposit. And if you have the risk appetite to leverage, the numbers start to look like equities rather than fixed income.

The Reserve Bank of India triggered this opportunity on June 5 when it announced a concessional foreign currency swap facility for banks. In plain terms, the RBI agreed to absorb the hedging cost that banks normally bear when they convert NRI dollar deposits into rupees. With that cost removed, banks can afford to offer substantially higher interest rates on Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits — and they are falling over each other to do so.

## The Rate Landscape Right Now

As of June 12, here is what India's major banks are offering on FCNR(B) deposits in US dollars for the new 3-to-5-year tenure buckets:

**ICICI Bank**: 6.50% across the board for NRI fixed deposits, effective June 11.

**YES Bank**: 6.50% for 3-year and 6.60% for 5-year tenures — currently among the most aggressive offers from major banks.

**Canara Bank**: 6.50% for both 3-year and 5-year tenures.

**Kotak Mahindra Bank**: 6.00% for deposits under $1 million, 6.15% for deposits above $1 million, effective June 11.

**Bank of Baroda**: Up to 6.00% on USD deposits, with 4.75% on GBP and AUD, 5.15% on CAD, and 3.75% on Euro deposits.

**State Bank of India**: The SBI Advantage FCNR(B) scheme offers 5.50% for 3-4 year tenures above $1 million, 5.75% for 4-5 years, and 6.00% for exactly 5 years. There is a 1-year lock-in.

**IDBI Bank**: 6.00-6.10% for 3-year and 6.10-6.20% for 5-year deposits.

**Smaller lenders** are pushing even higher: some are offering over 7% to compete for NRI dollar deposits, according to *The Hindu BusinessLine*.

## The Leveraged Play

Here is where it gets genuinely interesting for wealthier NRIs. Because the RBI has removed the hedging cost, private bankers are structuring leveraged plays where an NRI deposits a base amount and the bank lends additional multiples against that deposit.

According to calculations by Emkay Global Financial Services, an investor putting in $1 million and leveraging it nine times could generate annual returns of approximately $220,000 — a return of 21.8% on the original capital. Even at more conservative leverage levels of five times and three times, returns work out to roughly 15% and 11.6% respectively.

These are fixed-income structures delivering equity-like returns, and they exist purely because of the RBI's temporary subsidy.

## What You Need to Know Before Depositing

**Currency risk is eliminated.** FCNR(B) deposits are denominated in foreign currency, so you get your principal and interest back in dollars. There is no rupee conversion risk on your deposit.

**The window closes September 30, 2026.** The RBI's concessional swap facility is available only for fresh deposits and renewals raised before this date. After September 30, hedging costs return and these rates will likely fall.

**Lock-in period matters.** SBI requires a 1-year lock-in, and the scheme is available for 3-to-5-year tenures. Premature withdrawal penalties apply, and you should check each bank's terms.

**Tax treatment.** Interest on FCNR(B) deposits is tax-exempt in India for NRIs. In the US, however, the interest is taxable as ordinary income. You will need to report it on your US tax return and may be able to claim a foreign tax credit if any Indian tax is withheld.

**Deposit insurance is limited.** Indian bank deposits are insured by the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) up to Rs 5 lakh (about $6,000) per depositor per bank. For deposits significantly larger than that, you are taking bank credit risk. Stick with well-capitalised banks if you are putting in serious money.

## The Bigger Picture

The RBI's move is not charity toward NRIs. India needs dollars. The rupee has weakened more than 5% since January, squeezed by elevated oil prices from the Iran conflict and a record $30 billion in foreign portfolio investor outflows from equities. Higher crude prices widen India's current account deficit, and NRI deposits are one of the fastest ways to shore up the country's foreign exchange reserves.

Jefferies estimates the scheme could attract $50-70 billion in foreign currency inflows. If that materialises, it would substantially ease pressure on the rupee and give the RBI more room to manage monetary policy.

For NRIs, the calculus is straightforward: if you were going to hold dollars in a US money market fund earning 4-4.5%, you can now earn 6-7% in an Indian bank with zero currency risk and full repatriation rights. The window is narrow, the rates are unprecedented, and the math works. The question is whether you move before September or after — and after, the numbers will not look like this.
